Home News Arts and Culture Business Sports Opinion Research Live TV/Radio Media Elections Dark Mode Dark mode --> Photo Story GPNet celebrates member Nii Adjei Mensahfio on winning the GJA Best Online Documentary Award Source : Judy Yayra Avanu 20 November 2026 9:35am ▶ Listen to this article Audio By Carbonatix
The Ghana Photojournalist Network (GPNet) has congratulated its member, Nii Adjei Mensahfio, on winning the Best in Online Documentary award at the recently held Ghana Journalists Association (GJA) Media Awards, describing his achievement as a source of pride for the network.
Mr Mensahfio, a freelance journalist, received the recognition for his documentary, “Poaching, Bush Burning: Mole National Park's Conservation Scars”, which exposes the threats facing wildlife and the natural environment at the Mole National Park.
President of the network, David Andoh, commended the award-winning journalist for his achievement and encouraged him to continue producing impactful work.
“He has done well; he has made us proud, and he should continue to work to achieve more for himself and also for the network,” he said.
Mr Andoh expressed confidence that the award would be the beginning of more achievements for Mr Mensahfio and urged other members to work hard towards winning recognition at both local and international levels.
For Mr Mensahfio, the award was a mixture of surprise, uncertainty and fulfilment, particularly as he had set himself the goal of winning a GJA award.
Recounting how he received the news, he said a colleague, Ridwan Karim Dini- Osman of EIB Network, first congratulated him through a WhatsApp message.
“I was a bit shocked. I said, ‘wow, okay., Then in a moment I was like, ‘okay, so I won the award’,” he recalled.
He said the moment became even more special because his mother was present at the ceremony to witness his achievement.
“After the day, it was all pride and achievement. When I say pride, I don’t mean ‘arrogant’. I mean pride in the sense that I was happy and fulfilled with my work and the results it came with,” he said.
Mr Mensahfio said his interest in documentary photography and commitment to climate journalism inspired him to investigate the conservation challenges at Mole National Park.
The story emerged during a training programme with the Centre for Journalism, Innovation and Development (CJID), where participants were required to pitch story ideas for a grant.
Concerned about poaching, hunting and the burning of vegetation within the park, he decided to use his camera and writing skills to draw attention to the threats facing Ghana's wildlife.
“I find myself enjoying photographic living. I'm mostly interested in documentary photography. I enjoy being around new people, new environments, new worlds,” he said.
One of the most disturbing experiences during the project was seeing an elephant that had lost its tusk, an encounter that reinforced his determination to tell the story.
Although he initially hoped the documentary would attract widespread attention, it did not; however, the GJA recognition shed more light on the story, sparking renewed public interest, with more people requesting links to the work.
He particularly commended MyJoyOnline and Daily Gist for publishing the documentary and helping give it visibility.
“I want to give a big shout-out and a big thank you to MyJoyOnline and Daily Gist for giving the story life without subjecting me to any rigorous interrogation,” he said.
He praised MyJoyOnline for publishing the story with its photographs and captions arranged as he had submitted them.
He expressed hope that the award would draw further attention to the conservation challenges at Mole National Park and encourage meaningful interventions.
Beyond the recognition, Mr Mensahfio called on corporate organisations, development partners and individuals to support photojournalists, particularly those documenting environmental and social issues.
He said the high cost of cameras, lenses and other equipment, coupled with limited funding, continued to make field assignments difficult.
He cited the support of an experienced colleague, photojournalist Gershon Gbeve, who lent him an expensive lens for the Mole National Park assignment as he did not own one and could not afford one.
“We really need agencies and corporate Ghana to come on board and support people like me in the photojournalistic sector,” he appealed.
Mr Mensahfio also disclosed that his agency, ClimeScape Africa, a nonprofit providing free photography and videography training for young Africans interested in climate reporting at a global standard, is rolling out an initiative aimed at equipping young people with the requisite skills to document environmental challenges and the natural world through accurate and impactful visual storytelling.
The initiative, he intimated, is being carried out in partnership with Italian-based nonprofit - Associazione Culturale Vurria, and expressed openness to sponsorship and every other form of support for the project.
Encouraging emerging photojournalists to remain committed to their passion, he said: “Let your passion lead you, but let wisdom guide you.”
The Ghana Photojournalist Network says his achievement should inspire other members to pursue excellence and use photography to tell stories that contribute to public awareness and national development.
The Mole National Park is home to a vast number of wildlife species, including the Kob, also known as the African Antelope.
Some elephants in the Mole National Park were found with at least one tusk out of place, raising suspicions of poaching attempts
